subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.activity_title: Sky Watch: Drawing and Recording the Changing Sky
periods.textbook_anchor: Pictures of the Sky — Draw a picture of the sky as it appears in the morning, afternoon and at night (p. 152)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a brief, unhurried look around — what colour is the sky right now? Students share what the sky looked like when they woke up and what they expect it will look like after dark. The teacher draws out the idea that the same sky looks strikingly different at different times of day.

Students open Textbook p. 152 and work in the spaces provided to draw three sky pictures: morning, afternoon, and night. They choose colours carefully, capturing the Sun's apparent colour, any clouds, stars, and Moon as appropriate to each time. The teacher circulates, prompting: 'What colour is the Sun in the morning compared to noon? Where is the Sun in your afternoon sky?'

Students move to Textbook p. 153 and complete the observation table for morning, afternoon, and night, noting what they see in the sky, adding their own rows where the boxes already provided run out. Pairs compare their tables and discuss any differences in what they noticed.

A quick whole-class share: the teacher asks two or three students to describe one surprising observation. The class agrees on two things that are always true of the daytime sky (Sun is present and brightest; other stars are invisible). The teacher closes by naming the Sun as the sky's most powerful source of light and heat.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent observations of a natural phenomenon across different conditions through drawing and written recording.
periods.section_context: Sky colour changes at morning, afternoon, and night; Sun's apparent colour and position across the day; Sun as brightest sky object; stars invisible in daytime; Moon's apparent shape changes; drawing sky at three times of day; observation table for sky changes.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students what they notice about where the Sun seems to be at different times — this seeds the shadow investigation that the chapter builds toward. Encourage children whose home surroundings differ (open fields, urban rooftops, hilly regions) to share what their sky looks like.

periods.activity_title: Sky Diary: Tracking Animal, Plant, and Sunrise–Sunset Changes
periods.textbook_anchor: Pictures of the Sky — Have you observed any change in the activities and the behaviour of animals and plants at different times of a day? (p. 153)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses: 'Think about a rooster, a flower that opens in the morning, cows returning home at dusk — what is telling them what to do?' Students brainstorm briefly in pairs. The teacher collects suggestions and writes a few animal and plant examples on the board without evaluating yet.

Students open to Textbook p. 153 and discuss in small groups the changes in animal and plant behaviour at different times of day, then compile a shared list in their notebooks. Groups also address the Textbook p. 154 sunrise and sunset discussion prompts — how the sky looks, what birds and animals do, and what changes happen at home — noting their responses under 'Sunrise' and 'Sunset' headings.

Groups share one animal and one plant behaviour they found most striking. The teacher builds a class list on the board. The class then discusses how these changes connect to the Sun's light and heat — flowers opening to sunlight, nocturnal animals becoming active in darkness, lamps being lit at home after sunset.

Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one describing a sunrise change and one describing a sunset change that they personally find most interesting. The teacher asks: 'If the Sun stopped rising, what might happen to plants and animals?' — left as an open question to carry curiosity forward.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect observed changes in a natural phenomenon to the responses of living things in their immediate environment.
periods.section_context: Animal behaviour changes across the day (nocturnal animals, roosters, birds at dusk); plant behaviour changes (flowers opening); home activity changes at sunrise and sunset; sky appearance at sunrise and sunset.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Invite children to recall what their grandparents or older family members say about reading the sky or animal behaviour to know the time of day — traditional knowledge about animal and plant cues to time is rich and varied across regions. Keep the discussion grounded in students' own experiences rather than textbook-only examples.

periods.activity_title: Shadow Science: Torch and Stick Inquiry
periods.textbook_anchor: The Shadows — Take a torch and a stick; shine the torchlight on the stick and observe shadow changes when the stick moves and when the torch direction changes (p. 156)
materials: dark cloth or ability to darken windows
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 157 Sun-position and shadow diagram

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to think about their own shadow on a sunny morning versus at noon — is it the same length? In the same direction? Students share quick observations. The teacher names the investigation question: 'What controls how big and where a shadow falls?'

Working in small groups, students carry out the Textbook p. 156 investigation. They darken their workspace, hold the stick steady, and shine the torch on it. They first move the stick closer to and farther from the torch, recording how shadow size changes. They then hold the stick still and change the torch's direction, recording how shadow direction changes. Each group sketches two observations in their notebooks.

Groups share findings. The teacher guides the class to articulate two rules: (1) closer to the light source → larger shadow; (2) shadow falls opposite the light source. Students then open Textbook p. 157 and draw Sun positions and corresponding shadows in the spaces provided, applying these two rules to morning, noon, and evening situations.

The teacher briefly introduces the Jantar Mantar observatories and the Samrat Yantra sundial — ancient scholars used exactly this principle of shadows to tell time with precision, and Raja Jai Singh built these instruments across five Indian cities. Students note one thing that surprised them about what shadows can do.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use a controlled investigation to identify how the position and distance of a light source determine the size and direction of a shadow.
periods.section_context: Shadow formation with torch and stick; shadow size changes with distance from light source; shadow direction changes with torch direction; morning, noon, and evening shadow lengths and directions due to Sun's apparent movement; Jantar Mantar observatories; Samrat Yantra sundial; Raja Jai Singh.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups to predict before each step — 'What do you think will happen to the shadow if you move the stick closer?' — so the activity runs as genuine inquiry rather than demonstration. The Jantar Mantar connection works best as a natural conversational moment: 'People figured out these same rules long ago and built huge stone instruments to use shadows as clocks — can you imagine how?'

periods.activity_title: Moon Shapes and Star Patterns: Observing the Night Sky
periods.textbook_anchor: Night Sky — Observe the Moon in the sky and draw the shapes of the Moon you have observed on different nights (p. 160)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 160 Moon-shapes drawing space; textbook illustrations of Saptarshi star pattern

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Have you seen the Moon look like a full circle one night and a thin sliver another night? Has it ever disappeared completely?' Students share their own observations. The teacher writes the names Poornima and Amavasya on the board and asks if anyone has heard these words before and in what context.

Students open Textbook p. 160 and draw the Moon shapes they have personally observed on different nights in the spaces provided. Those who have observed a full Moon, a crescent, a half-Moon, and no Moon at all draw each shape. Alongside, students sketch any star patterns they have noticed — the teacher points out the Saptarshi (Seven Sages) pattern in the textbook illustration and invites students to draw patterns they recognise from their own sky-watching.

The class discusses Textbook p. 160 questions: Is there a pattern to how the Moon's shape changes? Are there nights when the Moon is not visible? The teacher guides students to recognise the repeating cycle — growing from crescent to full and back to invisible — and that ancient peoples used this cycle to count days and build calendars.

Students share which festivals their families celebrate that are tied to the Moon — the teacher connects Diwali to Amavasya, Rakshabandhan and Guru Poornima to Poornima, Eid to the first crescent. Students note in their notebooks one festival from their own community that is connected to the Moon or Sun.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record observed patterns in a natural phenomenon and connect those patterns to cultural practices in their community.
periods.section_context: Twinkling stars and star patterns in the night sky; Saptarshi (Seven Sages) pattern; Moon shapes — Poornima (full), crescent, half-Moon, Amavasya (new Moon); repeating lunar cycle; ancient calendars based on Moon phases; festivals tied to Moon phases — Diwali, Rakshabandhan, Guru Poornima, Buddha Poornima, Eid.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students: 'Does your family plan anything differently on a full Moon night or a new Moon night?' — this naturally surfaces regional festival knowledge without singling out any tradition. Accept all festival names students offer and write them on the board alongside the Moon phase they are connected to.

periods.activity_title: Chandrayaan and the Moon: Connecting India's Mission to Sky Learning
periods.textbook_anchor: India's Chandrayaan Mission — Give two differences between day and night, sky in morning and evening, our activities during day and at night, activities of animals during day and at night (p. 162)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to share anything they know or have heard about Chandrayaan — a spacecraft that India sent to the Moon. After a brief sharing, the teacher narrates: on 23 August 2023 the Vikram Lander touched down on the Moon's surface and collected data about what the Moon is actually made of. Students connect this to the Moon they have been observing and drawing.

Students open Textbook p. 162 and work on the written differences task — comparing (a) day and night, (b) sky in morning and evening, (c) our activities during day and night, (d) animal activities during day and night. They write at least two differences for each pair in their notebooks. Partners check each other's responses and add any differences they missed.

The class discusses their differences together. The teacher connects observations to the chapter's ideas: why is the sky different in the morning versus evening (Sun's position and angle), why do animals behave differently (light and heat from the Sun), and how does all of this relate to what a spacecraft orbiting the Moon would observe — continuous darkness on one side, intense sunlight on the other.

Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'One thing I now know about the Moon that I did not know before.' The teacher collects two or three responses aloud, celebrating curiosity about the sky.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate systematic differences between conditions of a natural phenomenon and relate those differences to changes in living things' behaviour.
periods.section_context: Chandrayaan mission; Vikram Lander landing on 23 August 2023; Moon surface data; differences between day and night; differences between morning sky and evening sky; differences in human activities during day and night; differences in animal activities during day and night.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'If the Moon has no atmosphere and is always either in full sunlight or complete darkness, how might animals or plants survive there?' — this encourages speculative scientific thinking while keeping the conversation grounded in what the chapter has already established about light, heat, and living behaviour.

periods.activity_title: Questions, Shadows, and Sky Poetry: Expressing Sky Understanding
periods.textbook_anchor: India's Chandrayaan Mission — Write your own poem inspired by the beauty of the sky (p. 163)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 162 and work on the enquiry task: Meera is curious about the teacher's statement that the Sun appears to move from East to West. Students list at least two questions Meera could ask. Partners share their questions; the teacher picks a few and asks the class whether these are good scientific questions — do they point to something observable and testable?

Students tackle the Textbook p. 163 shadow reasoning task — explaining in writing why their shadow points in one direction in the morning and another in the afternoon, and whether its length would be the same at both times. The teacher draws out answers from volunteers: the Sun's position in the east in the morning casts shadows westward; at noon the Sun is overhead and shadows are shortest.

Students open Textbook p. 163 and write their own sky-inspired poem in their notebooks. The teacher shares one or two starter lines as optional sparks ('The sky at dawn is…', 'At midnight the stars…') but emphasises that each student's poem should reflect their own sky observations from the chapter — colours, Moon shapes, shadows, or the wonder of a spacecraft landing on the Moon. Students who finish early may illustrate their poem or attempt the riddle on the same page.

Three or four volunteers read their poems aloud. The teacher affirms the variety of images — some students may have written about sunsets, others about the full Moon, others about shadows — and points out that this is exactly what scientists and artists both do: observe carefully and then express what they see.

periods.implied_lo: Students can formulate inquiry questions about an observed natural phenomenon and express their observations through a creative written form.
periods.section_context: Formulating questions about the Sun's apparent East-to-West movement; shadow direction and length at morning versus afternoon explained through Sun's position; sky-inspired original poem; shadow riddle.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: For the poem, reassure students that there is no single correct poem — any image drawn from genuine observation (the sky's colour, the Moon's shape, a shadow stretching long at sunset) is a valid and strong response. For the shadow reasoning task, ask: 'Can you point to where the Sun is right now? Which way would your shadow fall?' — using the actual classroom moment as data.

assessment_items.task: Think about the sky you saw this morning or last night. Choose one time of day — morning, afternoon, or night — and draw what the sky looked like. Below your drawing, write three things you noticed: the colour of the sky, where the Sun or Moon was, and one other thing you observed.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My chosen time: ___
My sky drawing: [drawing space]
1. The colour of the sky was: ___
2. The Sun / Moon (circle one) was: ___
3. One other thing I noticed: ___
format_of_output: drawing of the sky at one time of day
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any accurately described or drawn sky — a vivid orange sunrise, a bright white noon sky, or a dark starry night are all valid. The key criterion is that the three written points match the drawn sky and show genuine observation rather than imagination alone.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent observations of a natural phenomenon across different conditions through drawing and written recording.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can translate personal sky observation into a coordinated drawing-and-writing record, showing that the two forms of expression are consistent and grounded in real observation.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold ensures the student commits to one specific time of day and then records three distinct observable details. Check that the drawing and the three written points all describe the same time of day.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: drawing shows accurate sky features for the chosen time (e.g. orange-pink horizon at sunrise, stars at night); written points are specific and consistent with the drawing. Weak: drawing is generic with no time indicator; written points are vague ('it was nice') or contradict the drawing.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with drawing may describe their sky entirely in writing. Students who find writing difficult may extend their drawing with labelled arrows pointing to what they observed.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The section's primary task is the paired draw-and-record activity on Textbook p. 152–153; this item mirrors that format to let the student demonstrate the same skill in an assessment context.

assessment_items.question_text: Name two ways in which animals or plants behave differently at sunrise compared to after sunset. For each behaviour, say what causes it to change.
expected_elements: One animal or plant behaviour that occurs at or after sunrise (e.g. birds begin singing or flying, flowers open, roosters crow, diurnal animals become active)
One animal or plant behaviour that occurs at or after sunset (e.g. nocturnal animals become active, flowers close, birds return to roost, lamps are lit at home)
A cause linked to each behaviour — sunrise brings light and heat from the Sun; sunset removes light and brings darkness
assessment_items.annotation: Accept region-specific examples — a student who mentions cows returning from fields at dusk, or specific local birds, is demonstrating valid observation. Regional variation in which animals or plants are named is expected and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect observed changes in a natural phenomenon to the responses of living things in their immediate environment.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

expected_elements: One animal or plant behaviour that occurs at or after sunrise (e.g. birds begin singing or flying, flowers open, roosters crow, diurnal animals become active)
One animal or plant behaviour that occurs at or after sunset (e.g. nocturnal animals become active, flowers close, birds return to roost, lamps are lit at home)
A cause linked to each behaviour — sunrise brings light and heat from the Sun; sunset removes light and brings darkness

assessment_items.question_text: Priya holds a stick still and shines a torch on it from one side. The shadow falls on the opposite side. She then moves the torch closer to the stick without changing its direction. What happens to the shadow?

options.label: A
options.text: The shadow disappears because the light is too close.

options.label: D
options.text: The shadow moves to the same side as the torch.

assessment_items.annotation: This item directly tests the first rule derived from the torch-and-stick investigation. Only the distance between light source and object is changed; direction is held constant, so shadow direction is a distractor check.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use a controlled investigation to identify how the position and distance of a light source determine the size and direction of a shadow.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has reversed the distance–shadow-size relationship, possibly recalling that moving away makes things look smaller and applying that incorrectly to shadows.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses shadow direction with proximity — they have not consolidated that shadow always falls opposite the light source regardless of how close the source is.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student holds a misconception that a very close light source is too powerful to cast a shadow, conflating brightness with the geometry of shadow formation.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the four Moon shapes below described in words: (1) a complete bright circle, (2) a thin curved sliver like the letter C, (3) a half-circle, (4) the Moon is not visible at all. Write the special name for shape (1) and for shape (4). Then name one festival that your community or any community celebrates on each of those two nights.
expected_elements: Correct name for shape (1): Poornima (full Moon)
Correct name for shape (4): Amavasya (new Moon)
One festival associated with Poornima (e.g. Rakshabandhan, Guru Poornima, Buddha Poornima, Karva Chauth)
One festival associated with Amavasya (e.g. Diwali)
assessment_items.annotation: Festival answers are region-dependent. Accept any festival the student correctly links to the right Moon phase — for example, Chhath Puja (celebrated on the sixth day after Diwali's Amavasya) is acceptable if the student explains the Moon-phase connection. Regional variation in festival names, including local language names, is correct and should be credited.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record observed patterns in a natural phenomenon and connect those patterns to cultural practices in their community.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Correct name for the full-circle Moon: Poornima
Correct name for the invisible Moon: Amavasya
One festival associated with Poornima (Rakshabandhan, Guru Poornima, Buddha Poornima, Karva Chauth, or equivalent regional festival)
One festival associated with Amavasya (Diwali, or equivalent regional festival)

assessment_items.question_text: India's Vikram Lander landed on the Moon on 23 August 2023 and collected data about the Moon's surface. On the Moon, one side always faces intense sunlight while the other side is in complete darkness. Using what you know about how the Sun affects plants, animals, and our daily activities on Earth, explain what conditions on the Moon would be like for any living thing trying to survive there. Give at least two differences between day and night on Earth that you would use in your explanation.
look_for: Uses at least two specific Earth day-night differences from the chapter (e.g. animals behave differently in light and darkness; plants need sunlight to grow; humans use artificial light at night)

Applies those differences to the Moon's permanent light and dark sides with logical reasoning (e.g. the sunlit side would be extremely hot with no shade or night; the dark side would have no light for plants to grow)
Mentions the Chandrayaan/Vikram Lander context or Moon surface data as the premise
Response is coherent and shows that the student is extending chapter learning rather than guessing
assessment_items.annotation: This is an application and reasoning item — there is no single correct answer. Credit any response that uses at least two chapter-grounded day-night differences and applies them logically to the Moon's conditions. Do not require scientifically advanced knowledge (e.g. vacuum, radiation) — the item is grounded in Grade IV chapter content only.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate systematic differences between conditions of a natural phenomenon and relate those differences to changes in living things' behaviour.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

look_for: Uses at least two specific Earth day-night differences drawn from chapter content (animal behaviour, plant behaviour, human activity, sky appearance)
Transfers those differences logically to the Moon's permanent sunlit and dark sides
Names the Chandrayaan mission or Vikram Lander as the context for the Moon's surface conditions
Shows reasoning rather than assertion — explains WHY the conditions would be difficult for living things, not just states that they would be

assessment_items.task: Write a short poem (at least four lines) about something you have observed in the sky — it could be the Sun, the Moon, shadows, stars, or the changing colours of the sky. Your poem should include at least one observation that you actually made or imagined making.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My poem is about: ___
[Write your poem here — at least 4 lines]
The observation in my poem is: ___
format_of_output: original poem of at least four lines
one sentence naming the sky observation in the poem
assessment_items.annotation: Accept poems in any language the student is comfortable with, including regional languages and transliterated forms. The observation named by the student must be plausibly connected to the poem's content — it does not need to be scientifically precise, but it should reflect genuine engagement with sky-watching.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can formulate inquiry questions about an observed natural phenomenon and express their observations through a creative written form.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can draw on their sky observations from the chapter and express them through an original creative form, showing that scientific noticing and creative expression are connected activities.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold asks the student to name their subject, write at least four lines, and then identify the observation embedded in the poem. The third field is crucial — it shows whether the poem is grounded in real noticing or is purely imaginative without connection to observation.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: poem contains at least one image that is clearly drawn from sky observation (e.g. 'the shadow grows long when the Sun goes low'); the named observation matches the poem. Weak: poem uses only generic or conventional imagery ('the sky is blue, the stars are bright') with no connection to specific observations; the observation sentence is blank or contradicts the poem.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find verse structure difficult may write in free verse with no rhyme required. Students who prefer visual expression may write two lines and illustrate them, provided the illustration clearly contains an observation. Students comfortable in a regional language may compose in that language.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The section's closing task on Textbook p. 163 asks students to write a sky-inspired poem; this item mirrors that task to let the student demonstrate creative expression grounded in observation.
